title: Letter 4
paragraphs: _To Mrs. Saville, England._
August 5th, 17—.
Something so strange has happened that I must record it, even though you'll probably see me before these papers reach you.

Last Monday, July 31st, we were nearly surrounded by ice. It closed in on all sides, barely leaving the ship room to float. Our situation was somewhat dangerous, especially with a thick fog surrounding us. We stopped and waited, hoping for a change in the weather.

Around two o'clock the fog cleared, and we saw vast, irregular plains of ice stretching endlessly in every direction. Some of my companions groaned. My own mind grew tense with worry. Then a strange sight suddenly caught our attention and distracted us from our own predicament. We spotted a low carriage mounted on a sledge, pulled by dogs, heading north about half a mile away. Sitting in it was a being shaped like a man but apparently of enormous size, guiding the dogs. We watched the traveler's rapid progress through our telescopes until he disappeared among the distant ridges of ice.

This sight astonished us completely. We believed we were many hundred miles from any land. Yet this apparition seemed to suggest that land wasn't as far away as we'd thought. Trapped by ice, however, we couldn't follow the track, which we'd watched with the closest attention.

About two hours later we heard the sea shift beneath us, and before nightfall the ice broke apart and freed our ship. We stayed put until morning, though, not wanting to encounter in the dark those large loose masses of ice that float around after a breakup. I used the time to rest for a few hours.

In the morning, as soon as it was light, I went up on deck and found all the sailors gathered on one side of the vessel, apparently speaking to someone in the sea. It turned out to be a sledge, like the one we'd seen before, that had drifted toward us overnight on a large piece of ice. Only one dog was still alive, but there was a human being inside. The sailors were trying to persuade him to board our ship. Unlike the other traveler, he wasn't some savage from an undiscovered island — he was a European. When I appeared on deck, the master said, "Here is our captain. He won't let you die out on the open sea."
When the stranger saw me, he spoke in English, though with a foreign accent. "Before I come aboard your vessel," he said, "would you be kind enough to tell me where you're headed?"

You can imagine my amazement at hearing such a question from a man on the brink of death — someone for whom my ship should have been the most precious refuge on earth. I told him we were on a voyage of discovery toward the North Pole.

Hearing this, he seemed satisfied and agreed to come aboard. Good God, Margaret! If you'd seen the man who bargained for his safety like that, your shock would have been immense. His limbs were nearly frozen, and his body was terribly wasted from exhaustion and suffering. I'd never seen anyone in such wretched condition. We tried to carry him to the cabin, but as soon as he left the fresh air he fainted. We brought him back on deck and revived him by rubbing him with brandy and forcing him to swallow a little. As soon as he showed signs of life, we wrapped him in blankets and placed him near the kitchen stove chimney. Gradually he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.

Two days passed before he was able to speak. I often feared his suffering had damaged his mind. When he'd recovered somewhat, I moved him to my own cabin and attended to him as much as my duties allowed. I've never met a more fascinating person. His eyes usually have a wild, even mad expression. But when someone shows him kindness or does him the smallest service, his whole face lights up with such warmth and sweetness that I've never seen its equal. Yet he's generally melancholy and despairing. Sometimes he grinds his teeth, as if he could not bear the weight of misery pressing on him.

When my guest had improved a little, I had great difficulty keeping the men away. They wanted to ask him a thousand questions. But I wouldn't let them torment him with idle curiosity while his recovery clearly depended on complete rest. Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he'd come so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.
His expression instantly turned to the deepest gloom. "To find someone who fled from me," he replied.
"And did the man you were chasing travel the same way?"
"Yes."
"Then I think we saw him. The day before we found you, we saw dogs pulling a sledge with a man in it across the ice."

This roused the stranger's interest. He asked many questions about the route the demon — as he called him — had taken. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, "I've no doubt stirred your curiosity, as well as these good people's. But you're too considerate to press me with questions."
"Of course. It would be rude and heartless of me to trouble you with my own curiosity."
"And yet you rescued me from a strange and dangerous situation. You kindly restored me to life."

Soon after, he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I said I couldn't be certain. The ice hadn't broken until near midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety before then. But I couldn't say for sure.

From that moment, new life seemed to animate the stranger's failing body. He was desperate to go on deck and watch for the sledge that had appeared before. But I've persuaded him to stay in the cabin — he's far too weak to endure the raw air. I promised that someone would keep watch and notify him instantly if anything new appeared.

That's my account of this strange event up to now. The stranger has gradually improved in health but remains very silent and uneasy when anyone but me enters his cabin. Yet his manner is so gentle and agreeable that all the sailors are interested in him, despite having little contact with him. For my own part, I've begun to love him like a brother. His constant, deep grief fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble person in better days, for even now, in his ruined state, he's remarkably attractive and kind.
I said in an earlier letter, dear Margaret, that I'd find no friend on the open ocean. Yet I've found a man who, before misery broke his spirit, I would have been happy to call a brother of my heart.
I'll continue writing about the stranger whenever something new happens.
August 13th, 17—.

My affection for my guest grows every day. He stirs both my admiration and my pity to an astonishing degree. How can I watch such a noble person destroyed by misery without feeling the sharpest grief? He's so gentle, yet so wise. His mind is so refined. When he speaks, though he chooses his words with the greatest art, they flow with remarkable speed and unmatched eloquence.

He's now much recovered from his illness and spends most of his time on deck, apparently watching for the sledge that came before his own. Yet despite his unhappiness, he's not so consumed by his own misery that he can't take a deep interest in others' projects. He's talked with me many times about mine, which I've shared with him openly. He listened closely to all my arguments for eventual success and to every detail of the measures I'd taken to ensure it. His sympathy easily led me to speak from the heart — to express the burning passion of my soul and to declare, with all the fervor that drives me, how gladly I would sacrifice my fortune, my existence, my every hope to further my enterprise. One man's life or death was only a small price to pay for the knowledge I sought, and for the mastery I would win over nature's forces — the enemies of our race — and hand down to those who came after. As I spoke, a dark shadow spread over my listener's face. At first I saw him try to suppress his emotion. He put his hands over his eyes. My voice faltered as I watched tears streaming between his fingers. A groan burst from his heaving chest. I paused. Finally, in a broken voice, he said: "Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you also drunk the intoxicating draught? Listen to me — let me tell you my story, and you'll dash the cup from your lips!"

Such words, as you can imagine, intensely stirred my curiosity. But the wave of grief that had seized him overwhelmed his weakened body. Many hours of rest and quiet conversation were needed before he regained his composure.

Having mastered his emotions, he seemed to despise himself for being a slave to passion. Pushing aside the dark grip of despair, he led the conversation back to me. He asked about my earlier years. My story was quickly told, but it sparked many reflections. I spoke of my longing for a friend, my thirst for a deeper connection with a kindred mind than I'd ever found. I expressed my conviction that a man who didn't enjoy this blessing could claim little real happiness.

"I agree with you," the stranger replied. "We are incomplete creatures, only half-formed, if someone wiser, better, dearer than ourselves — the kind of person a friend should be — doesn't lend their help to perfect our weak and flawed natures. I once had a friend, the noblest of human beings, and so I'm qualified to judge what friendship is. You have hope. The world lies before you. You have no cause for despair. But I — I've lost everything and cannot begin life again."
As he said this, his face settled into a calm, profound grief that pierced my heart. But he fell silent and soon retreated to his cabin.

Even broken in spirit as he is, no one feels the beauties of nature more deeply. The starry sky, the sea, every sight these wonderful regions offer — they still have the power to lift his soul above the earth. Such a person lives a double life. He may suffer misery and be crushed by disappointments, but when he retreats into himself, he becomes like a celestial spirit surrounded by a halo, within whose circle no grief or foolishness can enter.

Will you smile at my enthusiasm for this divine wanderer? You wouldn't, if you saw him. You've been refined by books and sheltered from the world, which makes you somewhat fastidious. But that only makes you better suited to appreciate this remarkable man's extraordinary qualities. I've tried to figure out what elevates him so far above every other person I've ever known. I believe it's an intuitive insight — a quick but unfailing power of judgment, a penetration into the causes of things unmatched in clarity and precision. Add to this an effortless way with words and a voice whose varied tones are music to the soul.
August 19th, 17—.

Yesterday the stranger said to me, "Captain Walton, you can clearly see that I've suffered great and unparalleled misfortunes. I once decided that the memory of these horrors should die with me. But you've changed my mind. You seek knowledge and wisdom, as I once did. I sincerely hope that fulfilling your wishes doesn't become a serpent that stings you, as mine did. I don't know if my story will be useful to you. But when I consider that you're following the same path, exposing yourself to the same dangers that made me what I am, I think you might draw a useful lesson from my tale — one that may guide you if you succeed, or console you if you fail. Prepare to hear of events usually considered extraordinary. If we were in tamer surroundings, I might fear your disbelief or ridicule. But many things will seem possible in these wild, mysterious regions that would make people laugh if they had never seen how endlessly varied nature's powers are. And I'm confident my tale carries within it the evidence of its own truth."

You can imagine how pleased I was by his offer, yet I couldn't bear for him to reopen his grief by recounting his misfortunes. I felt a burning desire to hear the promised story, partly from curiosity and partly from a strong wish to help him if I could. I expressed these feelings in my reply.

"Thank you," he answered, "for your sympathy, but it's useless. My fate is nearly sealed. I wait for one final event, and then I'll rest in peace. I understand your feelings," he continued, sensing I wished to interrupt, "but you're mistaken, my friend, if you'll allow me to call you that. Nothing can change my destiny. Listen to my story, and you'll see how unalterably it's been determined."

He told me he'd begin his tale the next day, when I'd be free. This promise drew from me the warmest thanks. I've resolved to record it every night, as closely as possible in his own words, whenever I'm not occupied by my duties. If I'm busy, I'll at least take notes. This manuscript will no doubt give you great pleasure. But to me, who knows him and hears it from his own lips — with what interest and sympathy I'll reread it someday! Even now, as I begin my task, his rich voice fills my ears. His luminous eyes rest on me with all their melancholy sweetness. I see his thin hand raised with feeling, while the lines of his face are lit from within by his soul. His story must be strange and harrowing — and terrible must have been the storm that struck the gallant vessel on its course and wrecked it — thus!
